questions.q: Which tool should store user passwords?
questions.explain: Passwords need a slow, salted, memory-hard hash. SHA-256 and HMAC are fast, so leaked hashes can be guessed at billions per second. Encryption can be reversed by anyone who gets the key.
options: scrypt (or Argon2id) with a random salt per password
SHA-256 of the password
AES-256-GCM encryption of the password
HMAC-SHA256 of the password with a server key

questions.q: You must store sellers' bank account numbers and read them back to pay them. Which tool fits?
questions.explain: You need the original value back, so it must be encryption, and authenticated encryption at that. Hashes cannot be reversed, and base64 is an encoding anyone can undo.
options: AES-256-GCM with a key from the environment and a random nonce per value
scrypt, because it is the most secure
SHA-256, because it cannot be reversed
base64, because the numbers are short

questions.q: A payment provider needs to prove to your server that a notification came from it. Both sides know a shared secret. What does the provider send?
questions.explain: An HMAC can only be made by someone with the key, and it changes if a single byte of the body changes. A plain hash can be computed by anyone, and sending the secret itself exposes it.
options: An HMAC of the raw request body computed with the shared secret
A SHA-256 hash of the body
The shared secret itself in a header
The body encrypted with base64

questions.q: Why is Math.random() wrong for password-reset tokens?
questions.explain: Math.random() uses a fast formula with a small internal state, meant for games and simulations. randomBytes uses the operating system's cryptographically secure generator.
options: Its output can be predicted from earlier outputs, so an attacker could work out other users' tokens
It is too slow
It only returns numbers between 0 and 1, which cannot be converted to text
It returns the same value on every run

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each byte is written as two hex characters (00 to ff), so 16 bytes become 32 characters.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: base64url swaps + and / for - and _, and drops the = padding, so the text can go into URLs and file names without escaping.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 256 = 3 × 85 + 1, so remainder 0 gets one extra byte value. Taking a random byte % 3 would make 0 slightly more likely: that is modulo bias, which randomInt avoids.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: randomInt(min, max) includes min and excludes max. With min 5 and max 6, the only possible value is 5. For a die you write randomInt(1, 7).

questions.q: Why should a UUID used as an order id not double as the secret in a "view your receipt" link?
questions.explain: A v4 UUID is random, but an id gets copied everywhere. Access should be granted by a separate token (32 random bytes) or by checking who is logged in, not by knowing an id.
options: Ids appear in URLs, logs, e-mails and support tickets; a secret needs to be a separate value that is treated as secret
UUIDs are not random at all
UUIDs are too long for URLs
UUIDs can only be generated once per second

questions.q: Why does the reset-token code store sha256(token) instead of the token?
questions.explain: The e-mail link holds the token; the database only holds its hash. When the link comes back, you hash it and look the hash up. Someone reading the database cannot turn a hash back into a working link.
options: So that a leaked database does not contain usable tokens
So that the token becomes shorter
Because tokens cannot be stored as text
So that the same token can be used twice

questions.q: A fast hash (SHA-256) is fine for reset tokens but wrong for passwords. Why the difference?
questions.explain: The speed of the hash only matters when guessing the input is feasible. Guessing 2256 possibilities is impossible at any speed; guessing the few million common passwords takes seconds with a fast hash.
options: A token has 256 random bits, so there is nothing to guess; a password is chosen by a person from a much smaller set
Tokens are shorter than passwords
SHA-256 is slower for tokens
Tokens are stored encrypted as well

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The same input always gives the same digest, and one changed letter gives a completely different one. A SHA-256 digest is 32 bytes, which is 64 hex characters.
options: true false 64
true true 64
false false 64
true false 32

questions.q: An old service checks file integrity with MD5. What is the problem?
questions.explain: MD5 (and SHA-1) no longer resist collisions. Use SHA-256 or SHA-512 for anything security-related.
options: MD5 is broken: attackers can create two different files with the same digest
MD5 digests are too long to store
MD5 is not available in Node.js
MD5 is reversible

questions.q: Why use createHmac("sha256", secret) instead of sha256(secret + message)?
questions.explain: HMAC was designed to be safe where naive combinations are not. Use the standard construction instead of inventing one.
options: SHA-256 allows length extension: from sha256(secret + message) an attacker can forge a digest for a longer message without the secret
HMAC is faster
The two produce the same result, HMAC is just shorter to write
SHA-256 cannot take two inputs

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An HMAC depends on both the message and the key. Without the right key you cannot produce the right value, which is exactly what makes it proof of origin.
options: true false
true true
false false
false true

questions.q: The provider signed raw. Your framework parsed it and you re-create the text. What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify drops the spaces, so the text differs from what was signed and the HMAC would not match. Verify the signature on the raw bytes first, then parse.
options:
false
{"amount":4500000,"event":"charge.success"}

true
{"amount": 4500000, "event": "charge.success"}

false
{"event":"charge.success","amount":4500000}

true
{"amount":4500000,"event":"charge.success"}

questions.q: A webhook signature is valid, but the same request arrived yesterday too. Which pair of defences handles retries and replays?
questions.explain: A replayed request is correctly signed, so the signature check cannot stop it. A signed timestamp limits how long a request stays valid, and a stored event id makes a repeat harmless.
options: Remember processed event ids (idempotency) and reject signed timestamps older than a few minutes
Compare the signature with === twice
Ask the provider to sign with SHA-512 instead
Encrypt the body before storing it

questions.explain: The comparison stops at the first mismatch, so the work done reveals how many leading characters are right. That is the information a timing attack measures.

questions.explain: timingSafeEqual only compares buffers of equal length and throws otherwise. Check the lengths first and return false yourself; a signature's length is not secret.
options:
true
ERR_CRYPTO_TIMING_SAFE_EQUAL_LENGTH

questions.q: An attacker sends the header zz12. What does this print?
questions.explain: Hex decoding silently stops at the first character that is not hex, which here is the very first one. The length check before timingSafeEqual turns this into a clean rejection instead of an exception.
options: TypeError: invalid hex

questions.q: What is the purpose of a salt in password hashing?
questions.explain: The salt is random and stored next to the hash; it is not secret. Its job is uniqueness: attackers must attack each hash separately.
options: Equal passwords get different hashes, so one precomputed table or one cracked hash does not unlock many accounts
It keeps the password secret even if the hash leaks
It makes the hash shorter
It is a second password the user must remember

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: scrypt is deterministic for the same password and salt, which is what makes verification possible. A different salt gives a different hash for the same password.
options: true false
false false
true true
false true

questions.q: Why should a web server call the async scrypt rather than scryptSync at login?
questions.explain: Both compute the same result with the same cost. The difference is where the work happens: the async version leaves the event loop free.
options: scryptSync runs on the main thread and blocks every other request for the whole hash; async scrypt runs on Node.js's thread pool
scryptSync produces weaker hashes
async scrypt is faster to compute
scryptSync cannot be used with a salt

questions.q: scryptSync(pw, salt, 64, { N: 2 ** 17, r: 8, p: 1 }) throws ERR_CRYPTO_INVALID_SCRYPT_PARAMS. Why?
questions.explain: Memory use is about 128 × N × r bytes. The default limit is 32 MiB, so recommended parameters require an explicit maxmem.
options: These parameters need about 128 MiB, more than the default maxmem limit, which must be raised
N must be smaller than 2<sup>10</sup>
The salt is too short
scrypt is not supported on Linux

questions.q: Why does the stored password value include scrypt$131072$8$1$ before the salt and hash?
questions.explain: Verification reads the parameters from the stored value. When you raise the cost, you re-hash each password at the user's next successful login.
options: So the cost can be raised later while old hashes still verify with the parameters they were made with
So attackers know which algorithm to use
Because scrypt refuses to run without it
To make the stored value longer and harder to crack

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The two strings look identical ("Chióma") but one uses a single accented character and the other a letter plus a combining accent. Normalizing before hashing makes them the same bytes, so the user can log in from any device.
options: false true
true true
false false
true false

questions.q: Which login error message is best?
questions.explain: Different messages let anyone find out which e-mail addresses have accounts. Same message, same status code, and ideally similar timing for both cases.
options: "Invalid e-mail or password" for every failure
"No account with that e-mail" or "Wrong password", whichever applies
"Wrong password, the first 3 characters were right"
The exception message from verifyPassword

questions.q: What does the authentication tag in AES-256-GCM do?
questions.explain: GCM is authenticated encryption: decipher.final() throws when anything was altered, so you never get silently corrupted or forged plaintext.
options: It lets decryption detect any change to the ciphertext, the tag or the AAD, and refuse to return data
It stores the key in encrypted form
It makes the ciphertext shorter
It records who encrypted the data

questions.q: One bit of the ciphertext is flipped before decryption. What does this print?
questions.explain: The tag no longer matches, so final() throws. Note that update already returned bytes: never use them before final() has succeeded.
options: rejected: Unsupported state or unable to authenticate data
decrypted: pay ₦45,000 to seller 17
decrypted: pay ₦45,001 to seller 17
rejected: bad key

questions.q: The vault encrypts each bank account number with the AAD "seller:17". What attack does that stop?
questions.explain: The AAD is not encrypted, but it is covered by the tag. Decrypting with a different context fails, so ciphertexts are bound to their owner.
options: Copying seller 17's encrypted value into another seller's row so payouts go to the wrong account
Reading the account number with the right key
Guessing the key
Reusing the nonce

questions.q: A developer uses a fixed all-zero nonce "because the key is secret anyway". What is the consequence?
questions.explain: Same key and same nonce produce the same key stream. The nonce is not secret, but it must be unique per message: use 12 random bytes every time.
options: XOR-ing two ciphertexts cancels the key stream, so knowing one message reveals the other, and tags can be forged
Nothing, the key alone provides the security
Decryption becomes slower
Every message decrypts to zeros

questions.q: Two messages were "encrypted" by XOR-ing them with the same stream. What does this print?
questions.explain: c1 XOR c2 equals p1 XOR p2 because the stream cancels out. XOR with the known p1 leaves p2. This is why a nonce may never repeat with the same key.
options: PAY 9
PAY 5
an unreadable string
PAY 4

questions.q: A config file stores the database password as base64 "for security". What is true?
questions.explain: Encoding only changes how bytes are written as text. Secrets belong in environment variables or a secret manager, not in files, encoded or not.
options: Anyone who reads the file can decode it instantly; base64 is an encoding, not encryption
It is safe as long as nobody knows it is base64
It is as good as a hash
It is safe because base64 is one-way

questions.q: Where should the AES key for the payout vault come from in production?
questions.explain: A key in code ends up in Git; a key next to the data leaks with the data; a derived value is guessable. Load it from the environment and refuse to start if it is missing or the wrong length.
options: An environment variable or secret manager, checked for exactly 32 bytes at startup
A constant in vault.js, so it never changes
The database, next to the encrypted values
A hash of the server's hostname

questions.q: A login code has 6 digits (1,000,000 possibilities). What makes it safe enough?
questions.explain: With 5 attempts, an attacker has a 5 in 1,000,000 chance. Without attempt limits, a million requests would find it. Rate limiting is what makes short codes work.
options: A short expiry and a small number of allowed attempts, so guessing has almost no chance
Using SHA-256 to store it
Nothing, 6 digits are always unsafe
Generating it with Math.random()
Sending it over HTTPS

questions.q: Write constantTimeEqual(a, b) for two arrays of bytes. If the lengths differ, return false. Otherwise look at every byte (no early return): combine the differences with XOR (^) and OR (|) into one number and return whether it is 0.
questions.explain: a[i] ^ b[i] is 0 only when the bytes are equal, and OR-ing keeps any non-zero bit. The loop always runs to the end, so the time does not depend on where the first difference is. This is the idea inside timingSafeEqual.

questions.q: Write parseSignature(header) for headers like t=1790000000,v1=ab12. Return { timestamp, signature } with the timestamp as a number, or null when the header is missing, the timestamp is not an integer, or v1 is missing.
questions.explain: Treat the header as untrusted input: it may be missing or malformed. Rejecting early, before any HMAC or JSON.parse, keeps garbage away from the rest of the code.

questions.q: Write parseStored(value) for the stored password format scrypt$N$r$p$salt$hash. Return an object with algorithm, numeric N, r, p, and the salt and hash strings. Throw Error("unknown format") if the value does not have exactly six parts or does not start with scrypt.
questions.explain: A self-describing format lets verification use the parameters each hash was made with. Refusing unknown formats loudly is safer than guessing.

questions.q: Write randomDigit(nextByte) without modulo bias. nextByte() returns a random byte (0 to 255). Discard bytes of 250 or more (250 is the largest multiple of 10 below 256) and draw again; otherwise return byte % 10. The test feeds fixed bytes so the output is predictable.
questions.explain: Bytes 0 to 249 give each digit exactly 25 times, so every digit is equally likely. Throwing away the rest (called rejection sampling) is how randomInt avoids bias. Passing nextByte in makes the function testable with fixed bytes.

questions.q: Write toHex(bytes) that turns an array of byte values into a lowercase hex string, two characters per byte (so 10 becomes 0a).
questions.explain: toString(16) writes a number in base 16, and padStart(2, "0") keeps single-digit values two characters wide. Without the padding, [1, 10] and [26] could produce the same text.

questions.q: The Web Crypto API exists in browsers and in Node.js as crypto.subtle. Use crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", bytes) (it returns a promise of an ArrayBuffer) to print the SHA-256 of "abc" in hex.
questions.explain: This is the official SHA-256 test value for "abc", the same as createHash("sha256") gives in Node.js. TextEncoder turns text into UTF-8 bytes, and the result must be wrapped in a Uint8Array to read its bytes.

questions.q: Compute an HMAC-SHA256 with the Web Crypto API: import the key with crypto.subtle.importKey("raw", keyBytes, { name: "HMAC", hash: "SHA-256" }, false, ["sign"]), then crypto.subtle.sign("HMAC", key, messageBytes). Print the result in hex for key "key" and the message below.
questions.explain: It matches the standard test value from the lesson, computed there with createHmac. Web Crypto is promise-based and makes you declare what a key may be used for (["sign"]), which prevents some misuse.

questions.q: Write gate(event, nowSeconds, seen) for a webhook whose signature was already verified. Return "too old" if event.timestamp is more than 300 seconds away from nowSeconds, "duplicate" if event.id is in the seen set, and otherwise add the id and return "process".
questions.explain: Math.abs allows small clock differences in both directions. The seen set stands in for a database table with a unique index on the event id, which is what makes a provider's retries harmless.
